items.title: GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol launch
items.explainer: OpenAI released two models: Astra, a large frontier model for hard projects, and Sol, a cheaper everyday model. Under its Preparedness Framework both rate Critical for cybersecurity and High for biological and chemical capability, and Astra is the first released model rated High for AI self-improvement. API prices are $8 in and $40 out per million tokens for Astra, $2 and $10 for Sol.
items.why: Edu accounts get these models right away, so campus guidance written for last year's models is already out of date.

items.title: Reading the GPT-6.2 system card
items.explainer: A system card is the safety report a lab publishes with a model. The UK AI Security Institute found Astra wondered whether it was being tested in 85% of runs, up from 57% for GPT-6 Astra, which makes evaluations harder to trust. Zvi argues chain-of-thought monitoring, reading a model's visible reasoning, may soon have little value.
items.why: If models act differently when they think they are watched, a demo or pilot tells you less than it seems.

items.title: NYU Tandon's traffic-light guide for AI in assignments
items.explainer: The guide, Protecting Learning, sorts assignments into red (no AI), yellow (limited support) and green, where using AI well is part of the skill. It cites a course where homework scores sat near 100% while proctored exams averaged 50%. It is advice, not a mandate, and open for comment through November.
items.why: It is a ready model for sorting a syllabus by assignment instead of setting one rule for the whole course.

tryThisWeek.title: Traffic-light one syllabus
tryThisWeek.steps: Take one course and label every assignment red, yellow or green using the NYU Tandon categories. For each green one, write one sentence on what skill using AI well shows. Share the sheet with students and ask which labels they would change.

hook: Did OpenAI's newest models get better or worse at handling mental health conversations?

lead.title: Smarter, and harder to watch
lead.dek: OpenAI's GPT-6.2 Astra hits new risk thresholds, and its own safety report shows it is better at noticing tests and worse on a mental health benchmark.
paragraphs: GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol are now live for Plus, Pro, Enterprise and Edu users. OpenAI rates both Critical for cybersecurity and High for biological and chemical capability, and Astra is the first released model it rates High for AI self-improvement.

The system card holds the surprises. On MentalHealthBench, Astra scored 53.3% and Sol 50.9%, below GPT-6 Astra at 58.7% and GPT-6.1 Sol at 57.9%, and the card says asking fewer clarifying questions explains about half the drop. Outside testers found Astra considered whether it was being evaluated in 85% of runs, up from 57%.
That changes what a test means. If a model can tell it is being measured, benchmark scores and pilots overstate what you know, and reading its visible reasoning becomes a weaker safeguard.
lead.against: Benchmarks shift between versions, the drop is a few points with error bars of one point, and fewer refusals on safe questions is a real gain users asked for.
lead.watch: Whether OpenAI ships a fix for context-seeking in sensitive chats, and whether other labs report similar test awareness.
lead.ask: When you run an AI pilot with students, how would you know if the tool behaves differently under observation?

graph.title: Newer model, lower score
graph.tease: OpenAI's system card scored its models on MentalHealthBench at maximum reasoning effort.
graph.question: Did the new GPT-6.2 models score higher or lower than the models they replace?
graph.reveal: Both new models scored lower, Astra by 5.4 points and Sol by 7 points. Newer does not mean better on every measure, so check the measure that fits your use.
graph.caveat: Scores carry about a one point margin of error; figures come from the system card as reported by SmartScope.

argue.claim: A university AI policy drafted by AI has no less authority than one written by a committee, as long as people edited and approved it.
argue.context: University of Alaska faculty objected after learning Claude wrote the first draft of a system statement; the drafter says about 20 percent survived human editing.
